Eastmoor chose to bat first and were immediately made to look fragile, because Ben Archer hit his new-ball length early and turned the first few overs into a squeeze rather than a launch. Milo Hart was first to go, caught by Felix Ward after a scratchy stay, and before the batting side could reset Jonah Reed was bowled as well, so the card already had two wounds while Aaron Vale was still trying to work out how much risk the pitch would allow. Caleb Frost, the captain and keeper, did not settle either, and when Kiran Malik had him caught after only a small bridge with Aaron, Eastmoor were twenty-two for three and in the sort of trouble that changes a batting plan from expansion to survival. The important point, though, is that Vale never let that early damage become emotional collapse. He did not suddenly chase the game with ugly swings. He narrowed his options, took what Westhaven released, and began rebuilding the innings in layers, first with Evan Miles, whose nine from eighteen looks modest but gave Aaron a few overs of company when the innings desperately needed time, then with Oscar Bell, whose arrival changed the entire tempo of the match. The stand with Evan was only twenty-five, but it stopped the bleeding. The stand with Oscar was the one that made the total possible. Oscar’s thirty-one from seventeen was exactly the counterpunch Eastmoor needed at that stage, one boundary, three sixes, and the kind of clean middle-overs hitting that tells the fielding side they have not actually won the innings just because they took early wickets. Aaron remained the calmer center, picking the gaps and letting Oscar attack the length balls that had started to sit up, and when that partnership reached forty-eight, Eastmoor had dragged themselves from the edge of a sub-hundred score into a position where the last six overs could still matter. Mark Martin’s run-out of Oscar at ninety-five was sharp and important, because without it the innings might have run away quickly, but Westhaven’s problem was that Aaron Vale was still there and still organizing the card. He added enough with Noah Pierce to push the score into the final quarter, and even when Henry Cole finally had Aaron caught for forty-six, the innings had already gained the one thing it had lacked at twenty-two for three: structure. Aaron’s forty-six from forty-three was not a spectacular innings in the pure hitting sense, but it was the innings that made every later contribution count. Noah’s seventeen, Felix Turner’s ten, and Theo Carter’s unbeaten fourteen all carried value because Aaron had kept the innings alive long enough for those smaller scores to matter. The final stretch still stayed jagged, with Noah caught, Felix run out, and only a last-ball nudge from Lucas Shaw taking Eastmoor to one hundred and forty-two for eight, yet that was a very different total from the one Westhaven had been threatening to force in the powerplay. Westhaven’s bowlers had a lot right and one thing wrong: they kept taking wickets, but they never removed the game from Aaron’s hands early enough. Archer’s two early strikes gave them the dream start, Malik and Miles Grant kept the middle honest, Henry Cole landed the crucial Aaron wicket, Leo Fraser and Edward-style support roles kept the late order under pressure, and Mark Martin’s fielding directly cut off two dangerous running phases. Still, ten wides and a few loose balls into Oscar’s arc gave Eastmoor just enough oxygen to survive the early collapse and walk off with a score that felt defendable if they bowled with discipline. Henry’s ten was not large, but the partnership was worth twenty-five and helped Westhaven move from immediate trouble into something approaching stability. Adam played with more attacking intent, eighteen from fifteen with three boundaries, and Mason kept the innings connected from the other end, so when they carried the score to sixty for three, Westhaven were not comfortable but they were alive. That is where the match truly turned. Once he went, the innings lost its center. Adam was bowled by Charles Anderson soon after, Leo Fraser followed to the same bowler, and Aaron Vale then entered the second half of his player-of-the-match case by trapping Paul Ellis and later bowling Kiran Malik. Westhaven went from a chase with shape to a chase full of fragments, and the difference between those two conditions is usually the difference between pressure and collapse. Eastmoor’s defense worked because the wickets arrived in the right order. Theo Carter damaged the chase at both ends, first removing the early batters and then closing it. Charles Anderson struck during the crucial middle disruption. Matthew Thomas cut off the first repair. Aaron Vale removed the lower-middle players who might have stretched the match into an uncomfortable finish. Ryan Cole added the ninth wicket, and the fielding unit supplied the most important moment of all through Mason Ward’s run-out. That run-out is the kind of detail that can disappear beneath bowling figures, but in this match it was the hinge: before it, Westhaven had a set batter and a path; after it, they had isolated hitters and a rising equation. The contrast between the innings is therefore clear. Eastmoor were in deep trouble early, but Aaron Vale gave them continuity and Oscar Bell gave them force. Westhaven also had one batter trying to provide continuity, but once Mason was removed, nobody replaced him for long enough to carry the chase. That is why Eastmoor’s one hundred and forty-two proved enough, and why a thirty-one-run margin feels fair rather than inflated. The match was not controlled from the first over by the eventual winner. It had to be rebuilt, defended, and won again through pressure. Aaron Vale deserved the award because his forty-six was the central reason Eastmoor had a total to defend, and his two wickets later arrived when Westhaven were looking for a final route back. Theo Carter’s four-wicket spell was outstanding, Oscar Bell’s counterattack was essential, and Westhaven had genuine moments through Archer, Mason, and Mark Martin in the field, but Eastmoor were the side that handled broken phases better. They survived their collapse. Westhaven did not survive theirs.
